claim: All experiments were performed in an OT-reporter mouse line designed to selectively express tdTomato in oxytocinergic neurons.
source: All experiments for this study were performed in an OT-reporter mouse line designed to selectively expresses a red fluorescent protein (tdTomato) in oxytocinergic neurons (Figure 1A, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the mouse model used for all experiments.

claim: 92.8 ± 0.8% of tdTomato expressing neurons in the PVN were immunoreactive for NP1 across all animals tested.
source: Overall, we found that a strong majority of tdTomato expressing neurons in the PVN were immunoreactive for NP1 (92.8 ± 0.8% across all animals tested, 93.2 ± 1.0% in males, and 92.4 ± 0.5% in females, n = four animals total, two male, two female, 2838 total tdTomato-positive PVN neurons evaluated, 1352 from males, and 1486 from females).
evidence: Quantitative immunohistochemical data is provided with specific percentages and sample sizes.

claim: OT-MCNs were categorized based on the presence of a transient outwardly rectifying potassium current (IA).
source: Once patched, PVN OT neurons were categorized as either magnocellular or parvocellular based on the presence or absence (respectively) of a transient outwardly rectifying potassium current, IA (Luther and Tasker, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study (Luther and Tasker, 2000) as the basis for this categorization method.

claim: OT-MCNs had significantly higher somatic input resistance than OT-PCNs (1836.87 ± 107.84 MΩ vs. 854.81 ± 73.92 MΩ).
source: We noted that OT-MCNs had significantly higher somatic input resistance than OT-PCNs (1836.87 ± 107.84 MΩ vs. 854.81 ± 73.92 MΩ, respectively, n=62, 22, t = 7.5, p<0.0001, unpaired two-sample t-test)
evidence: Statistical comparison with specific values, sample sizes, and p-value is provided.

claim: Whole-cell capacitance at −70 mV did not significantly differ between OT-MCNs and OT-PCNs.
source: while whole-cell capacitance at −70 mV did not significantly differ (Cm: 31.1 ± 1.4 pF vs. 29.82 ± 1.8 pF, n=62, 22, t = 0.5, p = 0.621, unpaired two-sample t-test).
evidence: Statistical test results showing no significant difference are provided.

claim: None of the core intrinsic electrophysiological features of OT-MCNs varied by sex.
source: Importantly, none of the core intrinsic electrophysiological features of OT-MCNs reported here varied by sex (See Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and legend).
evidence: The manuscript refers to supplementary figure data supporting this claim.

claim: Bath application of 30 mOsm mannitol for 5 min increased basal firing rate of OT-MCNs by 3.37 ± 0.55 Hz.
source: We found that bath application of 30 mOsm MT for 5 min (in the presence of glutamate and GABA receptor antagonists, see Materials and methods) increased basal firing rate of OT-MCNs by 3.37 ± 0.55 Hz (n = 9, t = 6.2, p = 0.0002, Figure 2A–B.)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: A 15 mOsm mannitol stimulus for 10 mins increased basal firing rate of OT-MCNs by 1.39 ± 0.55 Hz.
source: A smaller but longer lasting hyperosmotic stimulus (15 mOsm MT for 10 mins) increased basal firing rate by 1.39 ± 0.55 Hz (n=9, t = 2.6, p = 0.03, Figure 2B–C)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: 30 mOsm mannitol failed to produce a significant effect on firing rate in PVN OT-PCNs.
source: This effect of MT is cell type specific, as 30 mOsm MT failed to produce a similar effect in PVN OT-PCNs (ΔFreq: 0.7 ± 0.3 Hz, t = 2.49, p = 0.06, t = 3.58, p = 0.005 vs. effect of 30 mOsm MT observed in OT-MCNs, Figure 2C).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing lack of significant effect in OT-PCNs is provided.

claim: PVN OT-MCNs are directly osmosensitive.
source: the present results demonstrate PVT OT-MCNs are directly osmosensitive and highlight that a primary effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge, when observed somatically, is excitatory.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing direct effects of osmotic challenge on firing rate.

claim: Activity-induced calcium influx drops rapidly with increasing distance from the soma in OT-MCN dendrites.
source: This approach revealed that activity-induced calcium influx drops rapidly with increasing distance from the soma (main effect of distance, F1.6,,6.4 = 15.0, p = 0.005, one-way repeated measures ANOVA, Figure 3B, Figure 3C, blue trace)
evidence: Statistical analysis of calcium imaging data across distances is provided.

claim: OT-MCN dendrites lack the ability to actively propagate somatic voltage changes to distal locations under basal conditions.
source: suggesting that under basal conditions OT-MCN dendrites lack the ability to actively propagate somatic voltage changes to distal locations, and likely also have a relatively low membrane resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed drop in calcium influx with distance.

claim: Using cesium gluconate internal solution increased activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites overall.
source: Notably, in these conditions, we observed an overall increase in activity-induced calcium influx (main effect of internal, F1,9 = 30.55, p = 3.7 x 10−4, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Figure 3C, red trace)
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing different internal solutions is provided.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels are robustly expressed at distal locations in OT-MCN dendrites.
source: These results indicate that functional calcium indictor was present in the distal dendrites, and that voltage-gated calcium channels are still robustly expressed at distal locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased calcium response with cesium internal solution.

claim: OT-MCN axons reliably and actively propagate somatic voltage changes in cells filled with potassium gluconate.
source: The results of this experiment indicated that OT-MCN axons, unlike dendrites, reliably and actively propagate somatic voltage changes in cells filled with potassium gluconate (Figure 3C, green trace).
evidence: Calcium imaging data from axons compared to dendrites is provided.

claim: Significantly less loss of calcium response was observed in OT-MCN axons compared to dendrites at distances > 90 µm from the soma.
source: Specifically, a two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed a main effect of structure on activity-induced calcium influx (axon vs. dendrite, both recorded using a K-gluconate-based internal solution, F1,4 = 9.17, p = 0.04), while post-hoc tests revealed that significantly less loss of response was observed in axons compared to dendrites at distances > 90 µm from the soma.
evidence: Statistical analysis with post-hoc tests is provided.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels are expressed along the length of OT-MCN axons.
source: Interestingly, these data also highlight expression of voltage-gated calcium channels along the length of OT-MCN axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data in axons.

claim: A 15 min exposure to calcium-free ACSF reduced activity-induced calcium influx by 80.3 ± 3.5% in the proximal dendrite.
source: Specifically, we found that a 15 min exposure to calcium-free ACSF (see Materials and methods) reduced activity-induced calcium influx by 80.3 ± 3.5% when measured in the proximal dendrite (~25 µm from the soma, n=5, t = −22.9, p = 2.15 x 10−5, one-sample t-test)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: A 15 min exposure to calcium-free ACSF reduced activity-induced calcium influx by 67.9 ± 3.3% in the distal dendrite.
source: and by 67.9 ± 3.3% when measured in the distal dendrite (~125 µm form the soma, n=6, t = −20.75, p = 4.81 x 10−6, one-sample t-test).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: External calcium influx is the primary driver of the calcium signal observed in OT-MCN dendrites after somatic stimulation.
source: These results, presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, indicate that external calcium influx is the primary driver of the calcium signal observed in OT-MCN dendrites after somatic stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the calcium-free ACSF experiments.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge had a small inhibitory effect on activity-induced calcium influx in the proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs (−14.3 ± 3.37%).
source: We found that acute hyperosmotic challenge had a small inhibitory effect on activity-induced calcium influx in the proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs (−14.3 ± 3.37%, n = 13, t = −4.2, p = 0.001, one-sample t-test)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge had a much larger inhibitory effect on activity-induced calcium influx in the distal dendrites of OT-MCNs (−40.6 ± 4.23%).
source: but had a much larger inhibitory effect in the distal dendrites (−40.6 ± 4.23%, n = 20, t = 4.44, p = 1.1 x 10−4 vs. proximal, Figure 4B, Figure 4C, left panel, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for data separated by sex).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge did not significantly impact somatic membrane resistance in OT-MCNs.
source: Notably, these changes were not associated with any significant/detectable impact on somatic membrane resistance (baseline: 1355 ± 109.8 MΩ, after MT: 1256 ± 109.3 MΩ, n=38, t = 1.38, p = 0.18, paired two-sample t-test)
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant change is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge did not significantly impact voltage clamp current applied to the soma during the train.
source: or on the voltage clamp current applied to the soma during the train (94.9 ± 5.21% of baseline after MT, n=11, t = −1.0, p = 0.4, one-sample t-test).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant change is provided.

claim: The effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx suggest a site of action along the dendritic membrane.
source: Considered together, these observations suggest a site of action along the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of somatic effects combined with dendritic effects.

claim: In the presence of TTX, acute hyperosmotic challenge continued to preferentially inhibit activity-induced calcium influx in the distal vs. proximal dendrites.
source: However, under these conditions, we found that acute hyperosmotic challenge continued to robustly and preferentially inhibit activity-induced calcium influx in the distal vs. proximal dendrites (by −55.8 ± 6.53 vs. −10.5 ± 11.0%, distal, proximal, n=9, nine respectively, t = 4.51, p = 0.002, Figure 4C, right panel)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis in TTX condition is provided.

claim: Activity-induced release of modulators is not required for the effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge on dendritic calcium influx.
source: suggesting activity-induced release of other modulators is not required.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of effects in TTX.

claim: TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channels play no apparent role in supporting propagation of voltage in OT-MCN dendrites.
source: This result further indicates that TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channels play no apparent role in supporting propagation of voltage in OT-MCN dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in distal/proximal ratio with TTX.

claim: Activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites did not significantly change over 25 min of recording under constant bath conditions.
source: we measured activity-induced calcium influx exclusively in the distal dendrites after 15 and 25 min of recording under constant bath conditions and noted that there was no significant change when measured at either time point (−2.0 ± 3.8%, 4.6 ± 5.3%, at 15 and 25 min, respectively, n=4, 4; t = −0.52, 0.86; p = 0.64, 0.45, one-sample t-tests, Figure 4D)
evidence: Statistical tests showing no significant change over time are provided.

claim: Basal calcium levels changed by ≤ 6.1% in response to acute hyperosmotic challenge.
source: We found that on average, basal calcium levels changed by ≤ 6.1% in response to acute hyperosmotic challenge
evidence: Quantitative data on basal calcium changes is provided.

claim: Small changes in basal calcium levels were not correlated with observed effects on activity-induced calcium influx.
source: and that these small changes were not correlated with observed effects on activity-induced calcium influx (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Correlation analysis is referenced in supplementary figure.

claim: The effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx in current clamp were comparable to those observed in voltage clamp.
source: Further, the effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx as observed in both proximal and distal dendrites were comparable to those observed in voltage clamp (proximal: −13.3 ± 3.61%, distal: −38.3 ± 3.92%, n=7, 6, t = 4.68, p = 0.0007, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison between voltage clamp and current clamp data is provided.

claim: Despite having an excitatory effect on action potential frequency in the soma, acute hyperosmotic challenge preferentially reduces activity-induced calcium influx in the distal vs. proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that despite having an excitatory effect on action potential frequency as observed in the soma (Figure 2), acute hyperosmotic challenge also preferentially reduces activity-induced calcium influx as observed in the distal vs. proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs.
evidence: This synthesizes findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge reduced somatic current observed in response to exogenous glutamate delivered to the distal dendrite by 62.5 ± 10.1%.
source: Acute hyperosmotic challenge reduced somatic current observed in response to exogenous glutamate delivered to the distal dendrite by 62.5 ± 10.1% (n = 5, t = −6.17, p = 0.003, Figure 5C)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge had no effect on somatic current observed in response to a train of AP-like voltage pulses delivered to the soma.
source: but had no effect on somatic current observed in response to a train of AP like voltage pulses delivered to the soma (Δ current = −2.4 ± 4.53%, n = 10, t = −0.5, p = 0.612, Figure 5C).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant effect is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge reduced dendritic calcium influx produced by delivering a train of voltage pulses to the soma by −33.13 ± 7.5%.
source: Conversely, acute hyperosmotic challenge reduced dendritic calcium influx produced by delivering a train of voltage pulses to the soma (by −33.13 ± 7.5%, n = 10, t = −4.4, p = 0.002, Figure 5D)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge had no effect on dendritic calcium influx observed in response to locally applied glutamate.
source: but had no effect on dendritic calcium influx observed in response to locally applied glutamate (Δ Peak Δ F/F: 1.94 ± 8.7% of baseline, n = 10, t = 0.22, p = 0.828, Figure 5D).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant effect is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge consistently and selectively inhibits responses measured distal from the stimulus that produced them, irrespective of whether those responses are measured using electrical or optical techniques.
source: These results demonstrate that acute hyperosmotic challenge consistently and selectively inhibits whichever response is measured distal from the stimulus that produced it, irrespective of whether that response is measured using electrical or optical techniques.
evidence: This synthesizes findings from the dual stimulation experiments.

claim: The observed effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge are consistent with the hypothesis that it is directly modulating dendritic membrane resistance in OT-MCNs.
source: As such, they are consistent with the hypothesis that acute hyperosmotic challenge is directly modulating dendritic membrane resistance, and thus voltage propagation, in OT-MCNs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the experimental data.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge effectively inhibited activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites of OT-MCNs (−44.0 ± 8.0%).
source: We found that acute hyperosmotic challenge again effectively inhibited activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites (Δ Peak Δ F/F: −44.0 ± 8.0%, n = 5, t = −5.5, p = 0.005)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge produced a much smaller effect in the distal axon of OT-MCNs (−10.0 ± 2.3%).
source: but produced a much smaller effect in the distal axon (Δ Peak Δ F/F: −10.0 ± 2.3%, n = 5, t = 3.4, p = 0.027 vs. distal dendrite, Figure 6A,E).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical comparison is provided.

claim: The effects of acute hyperosmotic challenge demonstrate significant compartment specificity within individual OT-MCNs.
source: This result demonstrates significant compartment specificity within individual OT-MCNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects in dendrites vs. axons.

claim: In OT-PCNs, there was no significant effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge in proximal or distal dendrites.
source: In OT-PCNs, there was no significant effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge in proximal or distal dendrites (Δ Peak Δ F/F: −7.7 ± 4.3%, n = 5, t = −1.8, p = 0.147; 6.6 ± 3.4%, n = 5, t = 1.96, p = 0.12, respectively, Figure 6B,F).
evidence: Statistical tests showing no significant effects are provided.

claim: In CA1 pyramidal cells, acute hyperosmotic challenge produced a weak inhibitory effect in proximal dendrites but no effect in distal dendrites.
source: In CA1 pyramidal cells, we noted a weak inhibitory effect in proximal dendrites, but no effect in distal dendrites (proximal: −6.4 ± 2.4%, n=6, t = −2.7, p = 0.045; distal: −3.80 ± 3.5%, n = 6, t = −1.1, p = 0.33, Figure 6C,G).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: The effects of acute osmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites of OT-MCNs demonstrate cell type specificity.
source: These results effectively demonstrate cell type specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects across cell types.

claim: Acute reduction of osmolarity by 30 mOsm effectively increased activity-induced calcium influx in the distal dendrites of OT-MCNs by 32 ± 10.7%.
source: Indeed, we found that acute reduction of osmolarity by 30 mOsm (achieved by diluting the bath solution with water) effectively increased activity-induced calcium influx in the distal dendrites of OT-MCNs (by 32 ± 10.7% of baseline, n = 10, t = 3.0, p = 0.014, one-sample t-test)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Acute hypoosmotic challenge had no effect on activity-induced calcium influx in the proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs.
source: while having no effect in the proximal dendrites (−2.03 ± 3.18% of baseline, n = 10, t = −0.6, p = 0.536, one-sample t-test, Figure 6D,H).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant effect is provided.

claim: The effects of acute osmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites of OT-MCNs are compartment specific, cell type specific, and bidirectional.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the effects of acute osmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx, as observed in the distal dendrites of OT-MCNs, are compartment specific, cell type specific, and bidirectional.
evidence: This synthesizes findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Acute hyperosmotic challenge reliably and reversibly reduced eEPSC amplitude evoked by a minimal stimulator placed near the distal dendrite by 63.4 ± 8.7%.
source: We found that acute hyperosmotic challenge reliably and reversibly reduced eEPSC amplitude as evoked by a minimal stimulator placed near the distal dendrite (by 63.4 ± 8.7%, n = 8, t = −7.3, p = 1.6 x 10−4, one-sample t-test Figure 7A,C).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: The reduction in distally evoked EPSC amplitude was not associated with a significant change in somatic membrane resistance.
source: As in earlier experiments, this result was not associated with a significant change in somatic membrane resistance (n=8, t = −0.14, p = 0.90, paired two-sample t-test).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant change is provided.

claim: 15 mM mannitol reduced proximally evoked EPSC amplitude by 30 ± 9.6%.
source: Indeed, consistent with this hypothesis, we found that 15 mM MT reduced proximally evoked EPSC amplitude by 30 ± 9.6% (n=6, t = −3.16, p = 0.03, Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: The effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on proximally evoked EPSCs is significantly smaller than observed when using a stimulator placed near the distal dendrite.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, this effect is significantly smaller than observed when using a stimulator placed near the distal dendrite (Figure 7D, n=6, 8, proximal, distal, respectively, t = 2.55, p = 0.03).
evidence: Statistical comparison between proximal and distal stimulation is provided.

claim: Pre-treatment with 10 µM ruthenium red blocked the effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on basal firing rate in OT-MCNs.
source: We found that pre-treatment with 10 µM RR blocked the effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on basal firing rate as observed in current clamp (Δ action potential frequency: 0.28 ± 0.21, n=7, t = 0.5, p = 0.61, t = 4.0, p = 0.001 vs. response to same stimulus absent RR, Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Ruthenium red did not alter the effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx in either the proximal or distal dendrites of OT-MCNs.
source: Conversely, RR did not alter the effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on activity-induced calcium influx as observed in either the proximal or distal dendrites (Figure 8C–D, see text of legend for further details).
evidence: Data showing no effect of RR on dendritic calcium influx is referenced.

claim: Ruthenium red did not block the inhibitory effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge on distally evoked EPSCs.
source: Similarly, RR also did not block the inhibitory effect of acute hyperosmotic challenge observed on distally evoked EPSCs (Δ EPSC amplitude: −71.5 ± 6.0%, n=6, t = −11.9, p<0.001, t = 0.72, p = 0.49 vs. effect observed absent RR, See Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: PVN OT-MCNs express distinct osmosensors in somatic vs. dendritic compartments.
source: Collectively, these results reinforce the hypothesis that PVN OT-MCNs express distinct osmosensors in somatic vs. dendritic compartments and suggest that the somatic but not dendritic osmosensor may be a member of the TRPV family (see Discussion).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by the differential effects of ruthenium red.

claim: The effect of mannitol on activity-induced calcium influx in distal dendrites of OT-MCNs is blocked in cells filled with a cesium-gluconate internal solution.
source: Interestingly, we also noted that the effect of MT on activity-induced calcium influx as observed in the distal dendrites of OT-MCNs is blocked in cells filled with a cesium-gluconate internal solution, which suggests that the dendritic osmosensor may be cesium sensitive (See Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for additional details).
evidence: Data from cesium internal experiments is referenced.

claim: Bath application of 400 nM muscimol significantly reduced somatic membrane resistance in OT-MCNs.
source: Unlike acute hyperosmotic challenge, bath application of muscimol significantly reduced somatic membrane resistance (from 1178 ± 166.6 MΩ to 226 ± 43.5 MΩ, n = 6, t = 4.9, p = 0.004, paired two-sample t-test)
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Bath application of muscimol produced a tonic inhibitory current of 15.4 ± 5.42 pA in OT-MCNs voltage clamped at −70 mV.
source: and produced a tonic inhibitory current (of 15.4 ± 5.42 pA, n = 6, t = 2.8, p = 0.036, one-sample t-test) apparent in cells voltage clamped at −70 mV, consistent with tonic activation of somatic GABAA receptors.
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Muscimol preferentially inhibited activity-induced calcium influx in the distal vs. proximal dendrites of OT-MCNs (−75.8 ± 2.7% vs. −31.6 ± 6.4%).
source: However, importantly, like acute hyperosmotic challenge, muscimol preferentially inhibited activity-induced calcium influx in the distal vs. proximal dendrites (−75.8 ± 2.7% vs. −31.6 ± 6.4%, respectively, n=6, t = 5.6, p = 0.003, Figure 9).
evidence: Quantitative data with statistical analysis is provided.

claim: Dendritic membrane resistance in OT-MCNs is likely to be under constant and dynamic regulation even absent changes in osmolarity.
source: and notably, highlights that dendritic membrane resistance is likely to be under constant and dynamic regulation in OT-MCNs even absent changes in osmolarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the muscimol experiments.

claim: PVN OT-MCN dendrites are weak conductors of somatic voltage changes in basal conditions in both male and virgin female mice.
source: We demonstrate that PVN OT-MCN dendrites are weak conductors of somatic voltage changes in basal conditions in both male and virgin female mice
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites is subject to robust modulation by a diverse set of stimuli acting on distinct types of ion channels in the dendritic membrane.
source: and importantly, we also find that activity-induced calcium influx in the dendrites is subject to robust modulation by a diverse set of stimuli acting on distinct types of ion channels in the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Increases in peripheral OT concentration are both rapid and frequency dependent, with concentration closely tracking MCN activity.
source: A curious feature of the neurohormonal response to hyperosmotic challenge is that increases in peripheral OT concentration are both rapid and frequency dependent (with concentration closely tracking MCN activity), while increases in central OT concentration are temporally separated from peak MCN firing, often by over an hour (Ludwig et al., 1994; Ludwig, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increases in central OT concentration are temporally separated from peak MCN firing, often by over an hour.
source: while increases in central OT concentration are temporally separated from peak MCN firing, often by over an hour (Ludwig et al., 1994; Ludwig, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: OT-MCN dendrites contain many large dense core vesicles loaded with oxytocin that are subject to both activity and calcium-dependent release.
source: This is somewhat counter intuitive because like axon terminals, OT-MCN dendrites also contain many large dense core vesicles loaded with oxytocin, and these dendritic vesicles are also subject to both activity and calcium-dependent release (Mason et al., 1986; Pow and Morris, 1989; Ludwig et al., 1995; Wang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some peripheral stimuli (e.g. suckling) can drive more concurrent increases in peripheral and central OT concentration.
source: Notably, other types of peripheral stimuli (e.g. suckling) can drive more concurrent increases in peripheral and central OT concentration suggesting more synchronous release of OT from both axon terminals and dendrites (Neumann et al., 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: α-melanocyte stimulating hormone has been demonstrated to promote dendritic release of OT while actively inhibiting both firing rate and release from axon terminals in the neurohypophysis.
source: while some locally synthesized signaling molecules (e.g. α-melanocyte stimulating hormone) have been demonstrated to promote dendritic release of OT while actively inhibiting both firing rate and release from axon terminals in the neurohypophysis (Neumann et al., 1993; Sabatier et al., 2003; Sabatier, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The relationship between somatic activity and dendritic release of peptide in hypothalamic MCNs is likely subject to modulation.
source: Collectively, these types of data effectively highlight that although at least loosely coupled, the relationship between somatic activity and dendritic release of peptide in hypothalamic MCNs is likely subject to modulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on differential release patterns.

claim: Specific endogenous modulators acting directly on dendrites can prime dendritic vesicles to be more available for activity-induced release.
source: The most well-established basis for understanding this flexibility invokes a model of conditional priming, whereby specific endogenous modulators, acting directly on the dendrites, can prime dendritic vesicles to be more available for activity-induced release (Morris and Ludwig, 2004; Ludwig and Leng, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Maximizing calcium-dependent dendritic priming prior to hyperosmotic challenge increased the amount of dendritic release of OT without altering its time course.
source: However, in the specific case of hyperosmotic challenge, maximizing calcium-dependent dendritic priming prior to hyperosmotic challenge was found to increase the amount of dendritic release of OT, remarkably, without altering its time course (Ludwig et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Osmolarity modulates activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites by acting on osmosensitive ion channels expressed along the dendritic membrane.
source: Collectively, these data indicate for the first time that osmolarity modulates activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites by acting on osmosensitive ion channels expressed along the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This is a novel conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism of osmosensitive channels in dendrites may reduce activity-induced dendritic release of OT during times of high somatic activity induced by acute hyperosmotic challenge.
source: Based on these data, it is reasonable to postulate that this mechanism may reduce activity-induced dendritic release of OT during times of high somatic activity as induced by acute hyperosmotic challenge.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: TRPV channels are the only RR sensitive channels that have potential for osmosensitivity and are strongly expressed in the hypothalamus.
source: That said, to our knowledge TRPV channels are the only RR sensitive channels that have potential for osmosensitivity and that are strongly expressed in the hypothalamus (Sharif Naeini et al., 2006; Sladek and Johnson, 2013; Prager-Khoutorsky and Bourque, 2015; Zaelzer et al., 2015; Shenton and Pyner, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and knowledge of channel properties.

claim: The somatic osmosensor in OT-MCNs may be a member of the TRPV family.
source: suggesting that the somatic osmosensor described here may be a member of the TRPV family.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the ruthenium red experiments and literature.

claim: TRPV receptors are cesium permeant.
source: even through TRPV receptors are cesium permeant (Caterina et al., 1997; Puopolo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The somatic osmosensor in OT-MCNs is hypothesized to be a member of the TRPV family, while the dendritic osmosensor is, or is coupled to, a cesium sensitive and potassium permeant channel.
source: Thus, overall, we hypothesize that the somatic osmosensor described here is a member of the TRPV family, while the dendritic osmosensor is, or is coupled to, a cesium sensitive and potassium permeant channel.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings with cesium and ruthenium red.

claim: All novel aspects of OT-MCN dendritic physiology revealed in this study were identical in male and virgin female mice.
source: Next, it is interesting to highlight that all novel aspects of OT-MCN dendritic physiology revealed here, as well as most other core intrinsic features of OT-MCNs observed, were identical in male and virgin female mice
evidence: This is based on the lack of sex differences observed in the experiments.

claim: Novel aspects of OT-MCN dendritic physiology have a fundamental and sex independent role in regulation of oxytocinergic signaling.
source: suggesting that they have a fundamental and sex independent role in regulation of oxytocinergic signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of sex differences.

claim: Aspects of OT-MCN physiology relevant to central OT signaling could be regulated in a context and sex specific way.
source: That said, it seems plausible that aspects of OT-MCN physiology likely relevant to central OT signaling, such as the dendritic conductivity, could be regulated in a context and sex specific way.
evidence: This is speculation about potential context-dependent regulation.

claim: Concurrent increases in both peripheral and central release of OT have been reported in response to suckling.
source: Indeed, concurrent increases in both peripheral and central release of OT have been reported in response to suckling (Neumann et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation of dendritic osmosensors not only transiently reduces the probability of activity-induced dendritic release of OT into the CNS, but also simultaneously reduces the impact of descending central inputs forming dendritic synapses on MCN firing rate.
source: This finding, in combination with other observed effects, suggests that activation of dendritic osmosensors not only transiently reduces the probability of activity-induced dendritic release of OT into the CNS, but also simultaneously reduces the impact of descending central inputs forming dendritic synapses on MCN firing rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects on EPSCs and calcium influx.

claim: Changes in dendritic osmosensitivity are expected to effectively but transiently prioritize activity-induced increases in peripheral OT concentration.
source: These changes are expected to effectively but transiently prioritize activity-induced increases in peripheral OT concentration.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple types of GABAergic receptor subunits, including the typically extrasynaptic δ subunit, are expressed on MCN dendrites and/or in magnocellular regions of the PVN.
source: The later finding is consistent with prior reports that multiple types of GABAergic receptor subunits, including the typically extrasynaptic δ subunit, are expressed on MCN dendrites and/or in magnocellular regions of the PVN (Fenelon et al., 1995; Pirker et al., 2000; Belelli et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tonic GABAergic currents have been directly observed in MCNs.
source: and is interesting to consider along with the fact tonic GABAergic currents have been directly observed in MCNs (Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Endogenous regulation of dendritic conductivity may represent an important mechanism for regulating central OT concentration even in situations where osmolarity remains constant.
source: It is also important in the context of this study because it highlights that endogenous regulation of dendritic conductivity may represent an important mechanism for regulating central OT concentration even in situations where osmolarity remains constant.
evidence: This is inferred from the muscimol experiments.

claim: OT-MCNs receive significantly more frequent bursts of GABAergic IPSCs during lactation.
source: For example, it is intriguing to note that OT-MCNs receive significantly more frequent bursts of GABAergic IPSCs during lactation (Popescu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lactation has been associated with a significant positive shift in the reversal potential of GABA-receptor-mediated currents.
source: and that lactation has also been associated with a significant positive shift in the reversal potential of GABA-receptor-mediated currents (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Central OT signaling systems are a promising therapeutic target for a variety of conditions impacting mental health.
source: Finally, as noted in more detail in the Introduction, central OT signaling systems are a promising therapeutic target for a variety of conditions impacting mental health
evidence: This is based on the literature cited in the introduction.

claim: The best available current strategy for therapeutically modulating activation of central OTRs in humans involves intranasal delivery of an exogenous agonist that has low permeability to the blood brain barrier.
source: and yet the best available current strategy for therapeutically modulating activation of central OTRs in humans involves intranasal delivery of an exogenous agonist that has low permeability to the blood brain barrier (Evans et al., 2014; Leng and Ludwig, 2016; Quintana and Woolley, 2016; Quintana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A better understanding of OT-MCN physiology may ultimately lead to improved therapeutic options that better mimic natural aspects of central OT signaling.
source: In our view, a better understanding of OT-MCN physiology, particularly as it relates to release of endogenous OT in the CNS, may ultimately lead to improved therapeutic options that are better able to mimic natural concentration, kinetic, and context-dependent aspects of central OT signaling.
evidence: This is a perspective on the potential translational impact of the research.

claim: Measures of activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites reveal a novel aspect of dendritic physiology likely to underlie the flexible relationship between somatic activity and dendritic release of OT.
source: In the current study, measures of activity-induced calcium influx in OT-MCN dendrites reveals a novel aspect of dendritic physiology likely to underlie the flexible relationship between somatic activity and dendritic release of OT.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main contribution.

claim: OT-MCNs substantially outnumber OT-PCNs.
source: The current study focuses on dendritic physiology of PVN OT-MCNs because (1) OT-MCNs substantially outnumber OT-PCNs (Althammer and Grinevich, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Most axons of OT-MCNs project through the median eminence to the posterior pituitary where activity dependent release into the vasculature increases peripheral (and not central) OT concentration.
source: (2) most axons of OT-MCNs project through the median eminence to the posterior pituitary where activity (action potential) dependent release into the vasculature increases peripheral (and not central) OT concentration (Guzek, 1987; Robinson et al., 1989; Falke, 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A large portion of OT available for release into the CNS exists in dendritic rather than axonal vesicles that are subject to activity and calcium dependent exocytosis.
source: (3) a large portion of OT available for release into the CNS exists in dendritic rather than axonal vesicles that are subject to activity, and calcium, dependent exocytosis (Pow and Morris, 1989; Ludwig et al., 2002; Ludwig and Leng, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dendritic exocytosis supports functionally important peptide mediated paracrine signaling within the hypothalamus.
source: (4) such exocytosis supports functionally important peptide mediated paracrine signaling within the hypothalamus (Son et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2015; Pati et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dendritic release likely drives volume transmission to increase functional activation of OTRs in a variety of extrahypothalamic cortical and limbic areas.
source: and (5) likely also drives volume transmission to increase functional activation of OTRs in a variety of extrahypothalamic cortical and limbic areas (Veening et al., 2010; Fuxe et al., 2012; Ludwig and Stern, 2015; Brown et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dendritic release likely works in concert with limited/targeted release from centrally projecting axon collaterals of OT neurons.
source: Indeed, this mechanism seems likely to work in concert with limited/targeted release from centrally projecting axon collaterals of OT neurons, as has been effectively demonstrated in several extrahypothalamic areas to date (Knobloch et al., 2012; Eliava et al., 2016; Oettl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Central oxytocinergic signaling plays an important modulatory role in fear conditioning, stress responding, anxiety-related behaviors, maternal behavior, sexual behavior, and social recognition.
source: Significant evidence indicates an important modulatory role for central oxytocinergic signaling in a wide variety of processes including fear conditioning, stress responding, anxiety-related behaviors, maternal behavior, sexual behavior, and social recognition (e.g. see Bosch et al., 2005; Knobloch et al., 2012; Jurek et al., 2015; Veening et al., 2015; Neumann and Slattery, 2016; Lin et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2019; Valtcheva and Froemke, 2019; Winter and Jurek, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Animal models with genetic disruptions in OT signaling systems exhibit a range of social and behavioral deficits.
source: while conversely, animal models with genetic disruptions in OT signaling systems exhibit a range of social and behavioral deficits (e.g. see Jin et al., 2007; Young, 2007; Lee et al., 2008; Higashida et al., 2010; Pobbe et al., 2012; Kent et al., 2013; Morales-Rivera et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Caldwell et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Effective therapeutic delivery of exogenous OTR agonists into the CNS of humans remains difficult.
source: However, effective therapeutic delivery of exogenous OTR agonists into the CNS of humans remains difficult (Ermisch et al., 1985; McEwen, 2004; Veening and Olivier, 2013; Leng and Ludwig, 2016; Quintana and Woolley, 2016; De Cagna et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.
